report:
# Does Magnesium Supplementation Improve Depression Symptoms?

**Short answer: The evidence leans toward "yes," but with important caveats.**

## What the evidence shows

The strongest evidence comes from a 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published in *Frontiers in Psychiatry*, which pooled eight effect sizes from multiple trials. It found a statistically significant reduction in depression scores with magnesium supplementation compared to control conditions (standardized mean difference: −0.919, 95% CI: −1.443 to −0.396, p = 0.001) — a fairly large effect size ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10783196/)).

A widely-cited individual RCT (Tarleton et al., 2017, *PLOS ONE*) tested 248 mg/day of magnesium (from magnesium chloride) in adults with mild-to-moderate depression and found meaningful symptom improvement within just two weeks ([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0180067)).

A separate systematic review in *BJPsych Open* examined magnesium and mood disorders more broadly, noting that dietary magnesium intake showed an inverse association with depression in cross-sectional studies, though this relationship was less consistent in prospective studies — suggesting supplementation trials and observational dietary studies don't always agree ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/bjpsych-open/article/magnesium-and-mood-disorders-systematic-review-and-metaanalysis/9257DB9E4EAC7F0A5C5B84E63B4D3AEF)).

## Proposed mechanism

Magnesium acts as a natural blocker of NMDA glutamate receptors in the brain. Deficiency may lead to excessive receptor activity, contributing to mood dysregulation — a mechanism plausibly similar to how the antidepressant ketamine works ([nejm.org](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2206443) discusses ketamine's mechanism, referenced by other sources for comparison).

## Caveats
- The original RCTs feeding into the meta-analysis are inconsistent, with the *Frontiers* authors themselves noting "controversial findings."
- Most benefit is shown in people with mild-to-moderate depression or magnesium deficiency, not necessarily severe depression.
- Sample sizes remain small overall.

**Conclusion:** Current RCT evidence supports magnesium supplementation modestly improving depressive symptoms, though larger, more consistent trials would strengthen confidence.
